name: Electric Bicycle
description: A vehicle designed to be operated by human power with the assistance of an electric motor rated 750 watts or less, with fully operable pedals and two or three wheels, in one of three classes: pedal assist to 20 mph, throttle to 20 mph, or pedal assist to 28 mph. It counts as a bicycle.

restrictions.rule: Fully operable pedals, two or three wheels, and a motor rated 750 watts or less
Class 1: pedal assist only, ceasing at 20 mph; Class 2: assists whether or not the rider pedals, ceasing at 20 mph; Class 3: pedal assist only, ceasing at 28 mph
The motor must disengage when the brakes are applied, and on a Class 1 or Class 3 when the rider stops pedaling
A Class 3 must have a speedometer showing its speed in miles per hour
Riders under 16 may not operate a Class 3 on a public highway, but may ride as a passenger on one designed to carry passengers
Riders and passengers under 16 must wear a bicycle helmet; the rule is enforced with a warning
Since January 1, 2020, manufacturers must permanently affix a label stating its class, top assisted speed and motor wattage
restrictions.citation: Maryland Transportation Article §22-420, as enacted by Chapter 64 of 2019

restrictions.rule: Must not be modified to change its motor-powered speed unless the label's classification is corrected
Meets the CPSC's bicycle requirements (16 CFR part 1512)
A bicycle, not a motor vehicle, moped or motor scooter: no driver's license, moped permit or registration
Ridden wherever bicycles are allowed, and must use a smooth-paved bike lane where there is one; barred from expressways and from roads posted above 50 mph except on their shoulders
May be ridden on sidewalks unless a local ordinance prohibits it, yielding to pedestrians

A local authority or state agency may ban Class 1 or Class 2 from a bicycle path it manages; Class 3 is kept off bicycle paths unless they run within or beside a highway right-of-way or the managing agency allows it
On a natural-surface trail designated nonmotorized, the agency that manages the trail decides whether it's allowed

On state public lands, a 2026 DNR regulation opens multi-use trails to Class 1 only (and to adaptive e-bikes for riders with disabilities, up to 20 mph); other classes are limited to roads, parking lots and off-road-vehicle areas
